name: Sofia's immune system and breathing on a pollen day

parameters.label: Pollen count
parameters.explain: How much pollen is floating in the air today, on a simple 0–10 scale like a weather app's pollen bar.

parameters.label: Pace
parameters.explain: We breathe about 12 litres of air a minute at rest and up to about 100 litres during hard exercise — and the pollen comes in with the air.

parameters.label: Minutes running
parameters.explain: The longer she breathes pollen-filled air, the more pollen her immune system has to react to.

parameters.label: Where she runs
parameters.explain: Keeping windows closed during pollen season keeps most pollen out of the air you breathe.

parameters.label: Weather
parameters.explain: Hot, dry, windy days put more pollen in the air; rain washes most of it to the ground.

parameters.label: Sunglasses
parameters.explain: A hat and sunglasses help keep pollen out of the eyes. They protect the eyes, not the nose.

parameters.label: How strongly her immune system reacts
parameters.explain: In an allergy the immune system treats pollen as an intruder. People differ a lot in how strongly — some don't react at all.

parameters.label: Breathing at rest
parameters.explain: Most people take 12–16 breaths a minute at rest.

rules.S: round(clamp(sens * G * loc * wx * (0.8 * Brest + (100 - 0.8 * Brest) * pow(P / 10, 1.3)) / 10 / 18, 0, 40))

overlay.caption: more pollen in the air × more air breathed in → more for the immune system to react to

explain.summary: Sofia's immune system mistakes pollen for an intruder and releases histamine, which makes her sneeze and her eyes stream. Running hard doesn't cause the allergy — but it makes her breathe several times more air each minute, so far more pollen reaches her nose. Indoors with the windows shut, the same hard breathing brings in almost no pollen, so nothing happens.
rules: Air breathed in rises from about 11 litres a minute at rest to about 100 at racing pace.
Pollen breathed in = pollen in the air where she is × air breathed in.
Sneezing grows with the pollen breathed in and with how strongly her immune system reacts.
Itchy eyes depend on pollen in the air touching the eyes, not on breathing — sunglasses help them, not her nose.
Histamine builds up with the total pollen breathed over the run.

source.fact: We breathe about 15 times a minute (12 litres of air) at rest, and up to about 40–60 times a minute (100 litres) during exercise.
In hay fever the immune system treats the allergen as an intruder and releases chemicals into the blood; histamine is the main one. Sneezing, a runny nose and itchy, watery eyes are common.
Closing windows during pollen season and wearing a hat and sunglasses help keep pollen away from the nose and eyes.

Hot, dry, windy days are more likely to have a lot of pollen in the air; on cool, damp, rainy days most pollen is washed to the ground. Staying indoors with air-conditioning helps during pollen season.
Normal breathing at rest is 12–16 breaths a minute.

choice.why: Real counts are grains per cubic metre and differ by plant; a simple scale keeps the focus on the mechanism.

choice.what: Air breathed in curves up with pace (power 1.3)
choice.why: Breathing climbs more steeply at hard effort; this matches about 12 litres at rest and 100 at racing pace.

choice.what: A shut indoor room has 2% of the outdoor pollen
choice.why: Closed windows keep most pollen out; the exact amount depends on the building, so this is a teaching value.

choice.what: Sneezing is proportional to pollen breathed in
choice.why: More pollen landing in the nose means more immune cells triggered; real reactions level off at very high doses.
They block much of the pollen-laden air from the eyes but not all of it; the size is illustrative.

illustrative: Sofia's reaction strength (7 out of 10), her 40-minute run and the sneezes-per-hour numbers are made up for a fictional story.
The histamine percentage is a teaching scale.
provenance.studying: Why some people's immune systems react to pollen and others' don't is still being studied.

citations.title: Allergic rhinitis

does: Shows the allergy (immune system) and the breathing (lungs) as two separate parts that multiply together
Shows why the same hard run causes no symptoms indoors
Shows eyes and nose responding to different things
doesnt: Measure any real person — Sofia is fictional and the numbers are a teaching scale
Say whether anyone has an allergy, or what to do about one
Include asthma, pollution, or different kinds of pollen
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Sneezing is harmless, but wheezing, chest tightness or trouble breathing during exercise is a reason to stop and tell an adult.
